entry: System of interconnected canals linking major rivers and lakes in North and East China. It was an important transport route between north and south in medieval and premodern China and is the longest artificial waterway in the world. The oldest sections were completed in the early 5th century BC during the [[Spring and Autumn period]] to supply the states of Wu and Yue. Emperor Yang of [[Sui dynasty|Sui]] completed the network in 609, but forced labor for its construction contributed to rebellions that hastened the fall of the Sui. The canal proved beneficial under the Tang dynasty, and each later dynasty treated its restoration as a duty. The capital moved to Khanbaliq (now Beijing) under [[Kublai Khan]]. The main stem links Beijing with [[Hangzhou]]. The section south of the [[Yellow River]] remains in heavy use by barges carrying bulk cargo. The canal is a [[World Heritage Site]].

Largest channel in [[Venice]], Italy, and a major water-traffic corridor of the city. It is 3.8 kilometers (2.4 miles) long and 30 to 90 meters (98 to 295 feet) wide, with an average depth of 5 meters (16 feet). It makes a reverse-S shape from the lagoon near the Santa Lucia railway station to the basin at San Marco. More than 170 buildings line its banks, most dating from the 13th to 18th century, and reflect the wealth of the [[Republic of Venice]]. Only one bridge, the Rialto Bridge, crossed it until the 19th century.

Steep-sided canyon carved by the [[Colorado River]] in [[Arizona]], United States. It is 277 miles (446 km) long, up to 18 miles (29 km) wide, and reaches a depth of over a mile (6,093 feet or 1,857 meters). Several studies support the hypothesis that the Colorado River established its course through the area about 5 to 6 million years ago, and it has since deepened and widened the canyon. The canyon and its rim lie within Grand Canyon National Park, the Kaibab National Forest and tribal lands including the [[Navajo Nation]]. Native Americans have lived in the area for thousands of years, and the Pueblo people made [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimages]] to it as a holy site. President [[Theodore Roosevelt]] was a major proponent of its preservation. The first European known to have viewed the canyon was García López de Cárdenas, from Spain, in 1540.

Sovereign state in northeastern Europe that existed from the 13th century until the 1795 partitions of Poland–Lithuania. Founded by Lithuanians, a polytheistic nation of several united Baltic tribes, it became the largest European state by 1440, controlling an area from the [[Baltic Sea]] to the [[Black Sea]]. It incorporated large parts of the former [[Kievan Rus']], and it was multi-ethnic and multiconfessional. Under [[Vytautas the Great]] the state reached its greatest territorial extent and defeated the [[Teutonic Order|Teutonic Knights]] at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410. Jogaila signed the Union of Krewo in 1386, creating a dynastic union with Poland. The Union of Lublin of 1569 formed the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], in which Lithuania kept separate ministries, laws, army and treasury. Russia invaded the reformed Commonwealth in 1792, and in 1795 the territory was completely partitioned among the Russian Empire, the Kingdom of Prussia and Austria.

Late medieval Russian monarchy, also known as Muscovy, with its capital at [[Moscow]]. Before 1389 it was the Principality of Moscow. Daniel (r. 1263–1303), youngest son of [[Alexander Nevsky]], received the city as an appanage in the 13th century. Ivan I (r. 1325–1340) moved the seat of the [[Russian Orthodox Church]] from Vladimir to Moscow. Dmitry (r. 1359–1389) inflicted a milestone defeat on the [[Tatars]] in 1380. Ivan III (r. 1462–1505) absorbed nearly all of the Russian states, annexed Novgorod in 1478 and adopted the title of sovereign of all Russia. His defeat of the Tatars in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Tatar suzerainty. The fall of [[Fall of Constantinople|Constantinople]] in 1453 confirmed the nascent independence of the Russian Church. Ivan IV (r. 1533–1584) was crowned the first Russian tsar in 1547, formally establishing the [[Tsardom of Russia]].

Highest class of motorcycle road racing, held on road circuits sanctioned by the Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme (FIM). Grand Prix road racing is the oldest established motorsport world championship, and the FIM, founded in 1949, coordinated its rules. The top class, originally known as 500cc, has been called MotoGP since 2002, the start of the [[Four-stroke engine|four-stroke]] era. Its classes are MotoGP, Moto2 and Moto3, all using four-stroke engines. Giacomo Agostini has 15 titles across all classes, and [[Valentino Rossi]] holds the record for premier-class race wins, with 89 as of 2026. Since 2025 Liberty Media has organized the championship.

City and county seat of Kent County, [[Michigan]], United States. It had a population of 198,917 at the 2020 census and an estimated 201,183 in 2025, making it the second-most populated municipality in the state after [[Detroit]]. Grand Rapids sits on the Grand River about 25 miles (40 km) east of [[Lake Michigan]] and is the hub of West Michigan. Settled in the early 19th century, it was incorporated as a city in 1850. It became known as the "Furniture City" for its furniture manufacturing and as "Beer City USA" for its craft breweries. It was the childhood home of President [[Gerald Ford]].

Winning all four major championships in one discipline of [[Tennis]] in a calendar year. Winning all four consecutively but in different years is a non-calendar-year Grand Slam, and winning them at any point in a career is a Career Grand Slam. In doubles, a Grand Slam may be achieved by a team or by an individual with different partners. The four major tournaments are the Australian Open in [[Melbourne]] in January, the French Open in late May to early June, Wimbledon in late June to early July, and the US Open in late August to early September. The Australian and US tournaments are played on hard courts, the French on clay and Wimbledon on grass. Wimbledon, founded in 1877, is the oldest. In 1988 [[Steffi Graf]] won a calendar-year Grand Slam, including Olympic gold, and [[Novak Djokovic]] holds the record of 24 men's singles titles.

2001 action-adventure game developed by DMA Design and published by Rockstar Games, and the first 3D game in the *Grand Theft Auto* series. Set in the fictional Liberty City, loosely based on [[New York City]], it follows the silent protagonist Claude, who becomes entangled in crime while pursuing revenge. Its open-world design is considered a landmark in the genre, and its violent and sexual content drew controversy. Released in October 2001 for the [[PlayStation 2]], it was the best-selling video game of 2001 and has sold over 14.5 million copies overall.

2013 action-adventure game and the seventh main entry in the [[Grand Theft Auto]] series. Developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games, it is set in the fictional state of San Andreas, based on [[Southern California]]. Released in September 2013 for the [[PlayStation 3]] and Xbox 360, it earned $800 million on its first day and $1 billion in its first three days. It is among the best-selling video games of all time and has earned over $10 billion in worldwide revenue. Its depiction of violence and women drew controversy.

Action-adventure video game series, created by David Jones and Mike Dailly. It is developed mainly by Rockstar North (formerly DMA Design) and published by Rockstar Games, beginning in Dundee in 1997. The name is a term for motor vehicle theft in the United States. The games are set in fictional locales modeled on real cities,. The original map included Liberty City (based on [[New York City]]), San Andreas (based on [[San Francisco]]) and Vice City (based on [[Miami]]). The third main title, [[Grand Theft Auto III]], brought the series into three dimensions and an open world. The series has shipped almost 475 million units and is one of the largest cultural exports of [[Scotland]] and the [[United Kingdom]]. Its violence, adult content and cut material have caused controversy, while its main 3D entries are frequently ranked among the greatest video games.

Parent of a person's [[Father|father]] or [[Mother|mother]], either paternal or maternal. Grandparents are second-degree relatives who share 25% genetic overlap with their grandchildren. Every sexually reproducing organism has at most 4 genetic grandparents and 8 genetic great-grandparents. Around 30,000 years ago the number of modern humans who lived to be grandparents increased, and it is generally believed that keeping information across three living generations was a key consequence. When parents cannot provide adequate care, grandparents often become primary caregivers, and in traditional cultures they often have a direct role in raising children. Research associates grandparental support with better grandchild well-being. They also transmit values, skills and cultural knowledge.

Coarse-grained intrusive [[Igneous rock|igneous rock]] composed mostly of quartz, [[Feldspar|alkali feldspar]], mica and plagioclase. It forms when silica-rich [[Magma|magma]] with a high content of alkali metal oxides cools slowly and solidifies underground. Granite is common in the continental crust, where it occurs in intrusions ranging from dikes only a few centimeters across to batholiths exposed over hundreds of square kilometers. Granitic rocks are classified by the relative percentages of quartz, alkali feldspar and plagioclase, and true granite is rich in quartz and alkali feldspar. Most also contain [[Mica|mica]] or amphibole, although leucogranites contain almost no dark minerals. Granite is nearly always massive and tough, properties that have made it a widespread construction stone throughout human history.

[[Apple]] cultivar with hard, firm, light green skin and crisp, juicy flesh, originating in Australia in 1868. It was named after Maria Ann Smith, who propagated the cultivar from a chance seedling. The flavor is tart, often sour and acidic. It remains firm and mostly sweet when baked, making it a popular cooking apple for pies. The apple turns yellow when overripe. The USApple Association reported in 2019 that it was the third most popular apple in the United States.

Fruit, botanically a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], of the deciduous woody vines of the genus *Vitis*, generally occurring in clusters. Grapes are a non-climacteric fruit. Cultivation began approximately 8,000 years ago, and the fruit has been eaten fresh or dried as raisins, currants and sultanas. Grapes hold cultural significance for their role in [[Wine|winemaking]], and other products include jam, juice, [[Vinegar|vinegar]] and oil. The most widely cultivated species is *Vitis vinifera*, native to the Mediterranean basin, Central Europe and southwestern Asia. As of 2024, grapes are grown on approximately 71,000 sq km of vineyards worldwide. Global production that year was estimated at 77.7 million metric tons, with about 53% destined for wine and 45% for fresh table grapes. The grape and wine industry contributes over $323 billion annually to the U.S. economy, as of 2025.

Subtropical [[Citrus]] tree (*Citrus* × *paradisi*) and its large, sour to semi-sweet, somewhat bitter fruit, with segmented flesh ranging from pale yellow to dark red. Grapefruit originated in Barbados as an accidental cross between the sweet orange (*C.* × *sinensis*) and the [[Pomelo]] (*C. maxima*). It has also been called the "forbidden fruit." Its juice contains furanocoumarins that interfere with the metabolism of many drugs, prolonging and intensifying their effects. Such interactions can cause abnormal heart rhythms, bleeding inside the stomach, low blood pressure, difficulty breathing and dizziness. Global production exceeded 6.9 million metric tons in the 2024/25 season, led by China with 5.25 million tons.

Structure of objects, called vertices, in which some pairs are related and joined by edges. Vertices are also called nodes or points, and each related pair is an edge, also called a link or line. A graph is typically depicted as dots or circles joined by lines or curves. Edges may be directed, as when one person owes money to another, or undirected, as when people shake hands. Graphs are the basic subject of [[Graph theory]]. The word "graph" was first used in this sense by J. J. Sylvester in 1878, who called it a chemico-graphical image, reflecting a direct relation between mathematics and chemical structure. Graphs model relational systems such as social networks, transportation systems and molecular structures.

Set of ordered pairs (x, y), where f(x) = y, representing a [[Function (mathematics)|mathematical function]]. When x and f(x) are real numbers, the pairs are [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]] of points in a plane, which often form a curve. The graphical representation is also known as a plot. For a function of two variables, the graph is a set of ordered triples (x, y, z) where f(x, y) = z, which forms a surface in [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional space]]. Graphs are used in science, engineering, technology and finance, typically plotting one variable against another on rectangular axes. A graph is a special case of a relation and does not by itself determine the codomain, which matters when deciding whether a function is onto.

Branch of [[Discrete mathematics|discrete mathematics]] that studies [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]], structures used to model pairwise relations between objects. A graph is made up of vertices (also called nodes or points), joined by edges (also called arcs, links or lines). Edges may be undirected, linking two vertices symmetrically, or directed, linking them asymmetrically. The field's origins lie in Leonhard Euler's analysis of the [[Seven Bridges of Königsberg]], which showed that no closed walk could cross each bridge exactly once. Graph theory is used in [[Computer science|computer science]] for algorithms such as shortest paths, in transportation to optimize routes, and in chemistry and biology to represent molecular bonds and genetic interactions. Notable results include the Four Color Theorem, which states that any planar graph is 4-colorable.

Single-layer [[Carbon|carbon]] allotrope arranged in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice, the thinnest two-dimensional material known. Graphene is known for exceptionally high tensile strength and electrical conductivity, and a single sheet is nearly transparent. [[Graphite]], formed from many hundreds of stacked graphene layers, appears black because it absorbs all visible light. On a microscopic scale, graphene is the strongest material ever measured. Philip R. Wallace theorized its existence in 1947, and Hanns-Peter Boehm defined the term in 1987. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated it at the University of Manchester in 2004 using adhesive tape, and they received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work.

Profession, academic discipline and applied art of creating visual communications intended to transmit specific messages to social groups. It is an interdisciplinary branch of design and the fine arts, using creativity, innovation and lateral thinking with manual or digital tools. Designers use the aesthetics of [[Typography|typography]], compositional arrangement, ornamentation and imagery to convey ideas, feelings and attitudes beyond what language alone expresses. Its origins in antiquity and the Middle Ages were linked to the rise of printing in Europe in the 15th century and to consumer culture during the Industrial Revolution. As a distinct profession in the West, it became closely associated with [[Advertising|advertising]] in the 19th century. The term first appeared in a 4 July 1908 issue of *Organized Labor*, a San Francisco union publication. Demand for experienced designers has grown with new technologies, which require attention to human factors beyond the competence of engineers.

Specialized electronic circuit for digital image processing that accelerates computer graphics. It may be a component of a discrete graphics card or embedded on motherboards, mobile phones, personal computers, workstations and game consoles. Modern GPUs perform calculations internally, such as rotating and scaling 3D images, and can run custom programs called shaders. With hundreds or thousands of calculation units, they suit parallel problems, which has led to their use in [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] and in training [[Neural network (machine learning)|neural networks]]. In 2009, [[Intel]], [[Nvidia]] and [[AMD]]/ATI held the largest market shares, at 49.4%, 27.8% and 20.6% respectively.

Crystalline allotrope of carbon, consisting of many stacked layers of [[Graphene|graphene]], typically in excess of hundreds of layers. It is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions and occurs naturally in metamorphic rocks. It converts to diamond under extremely high pressure and temperature. Its low cost, thermal and chemical inertness, and conductivity of heat and electricity suit it to high-energy and high-temperature processes. About 1.3 million metric tons were consumed in 2022, mainly for refractories (50%), lithium-ion batteries (18%), foundries (10%) and lubricants (5%). Synthetic graphite, produced above 2,100 °C mainly through the Acheson process, exceeds 99.9% C purity. Mined graphite is exported mainly by [[China]], [[Mexico]], [[Canada]], [[Brazil]] and [[Madagascar]], in that order by tonnage.

[[Insect]] of the suborder Caelifera, a group with powerful hind legs for leaping. Grasshoppers are among the most ancient living groups of chewing herbivorous insects, dating to the early Triassic, around 250 million years ago. They hatch from eggs as [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]] and undergo five molts without complete metamorphosis. Most are ground-dwelling plant-eaters that protect themselves through [[Camouflage|camouflage]] or by flashing brightly colored wings when startled. At high population densities some species change color and behavior and form swarms, becoming known as [[Locust|locusts]]. Locust swarms can destroy crops over wide areas and have caused [[Famine|famine]] since Biblical times. Grasshoppers are used as food in Mexico and Indonesia.

American rock band formed in Palo Alto, California, in 1965. Its eclectic style blended rock, blues, [[Jazz|jazz]], folk, country, bluegrass, reggae and world music. Its fans, the Deadheads, freely exchanged live recordings, which the band encouraged by allowing taping. The band disbanded after Jerry Garcia's death in August 1995. Its only Top-40 single was "Touch of Grey" (1987), yet it remained among the highest-grossing American touring acts for decades. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1994, and [[Rolling Stone]] ranked it number 57 on its 2011 list of the 100 Greatest Artists of All Time.
